nodes.statement: The question of whether machines can think should be replaced by a less ambiguous one, rather than relying on common usage definitions which would absurdly lead to a statistical survey.
nodes.span: Instead of attempting such a definition I shall replace the question by another
nodes.status_reason: reader holds the distinction between a question of fact and a question of meaning, making common usage definitions absurd

nodes.statement: The 'imitation game' is introduced, where an interrogator communicates via text with a man and a machine, attempting to determine which is which.
nodes.span: The new form of the problem can be described in terms of a game which we call the 'imitation game.'
nodes.status_reason: text introduces the rules of the game

nodes.statement: The original question is replaced by asking whether an interrogator would decide wrongly as often when a machine plays the imitation game as when a man and a woman play it.
nodes.span: Will the interrogator decide wrongly as often when the game is played like this
nodes.status_reason: follows from replacing the question and defining the imitation game

nodes.statement: The imitation game successfully isolates intellectual capacities from physical ones, making physical disabilities irrelevant to the test.
nodes.span: The new problem has the advantage of drawing a fairly sharp line between the physical and the intellectual capacities
nodes.status_reason: follows from the physical separation established in the game's rules

nodes.statement: Specimen questions and answers demonstrate that the text-based method can cover almost any field of human endeavor.
nodes.span: The question and answer method seems to be suitable for introducing almost any one of the fields of human endeavour
nodes.status_reason: text provides examples of questions and answers

nodes.statement: Even if the game is weighted against the machine because a human could not successfully pretend to be a machine, a machine succeeding at the game renders this objection moot.
nodes.span: if, nevertheless, a machine can be constructed to play the imitation game satisfactorily, we need not be troubled by this objection.
nodes.status_reason: follows from basic logic that passing a harder test is sufficient

nodes.statement: It is assumed that the best strategy for the machine in the game is to try to provide answers that a man would naturally give.
nodes.span: it will be assumed that the best strategy is to try to provide answers that would naturally be given by a man.
nodes.status_reason: stated explicitly as an assumption for the game

nodes.statement: Only digital computers are permitted to take part in the imitation game as the machine.
nodes.span: Following this suggestion we only permit digital computers to take part in our game.
nodes.status_reason: stated explicitly as a boundary condition

nodes.statement: The question is not whether existing computers would do well, but whether there are imaginable computers that would succeed.
nodes.span: whether there are imaginable computers which would do well.
nodes.status_reason: stated explicitly as a boundary condition

nodes.statement: A digital computer consists of a store, an executive unit, and a control, intended to carry out operations done by a human computer following fixed rules.
nodes.span: A digital computer can usually be regarded as consisting of three parts:
nodes.status_reason: reader holds the concepts of memory, instruction, and program

nodes.statement: Digital computers can be constructed and can closely mimic the actions of a human computer.
nodes.span: digital computers can be constructed, and indeed have been constructed, according to the principles we have described
nodes.status_reason: reader holds that machines of the period could be built and programmed

nodes.statement: The fact that modern digital computers use electricity is of no theoretical importance, as demonstrated by Babbage's mechanical design.
nodes.span: we see that this use of electricity cannot be of theoretical importance.
nodes.status_reason: reader holds that machines can be built mechanically or electrically

nodes.statement: Discrete-state machines move by sudden jumps from one definite state to another.
nodes.span: These are the machines which move by sudden jumps or clicks from one quite definite state to another.
nodes.status_reason: text defines discrete-state machines

nodes.statement: Digital computers are discrete-state machines with an enormously large number of possible states.
nodes.span: digital computers fall within the class of discrete-state machines. But the number of states of which such a machine is capable is usually enormously large.
nodes.status_reason: follows from the definitions of digital computers and discrete states

nodes.statement: Digital computers are universal machines, meaning one digital computer can mimic any discrete-state machine if it has adequate storage and speed.
nodes.span: This special property of digital computers, that they can mimic any discrete-state machine, is described by saying that they are universal machines.
nodes.status_reason: reader does not hold the universality proof or computability theory

nodes.statement: The main question is equivalent to asking if a particular digital computer can be modified with adequate storage, speed, and programming to play the imitation game satisfactorily.
nodes.span: either of these questions is equivalent to this
nodes.status_reason: follows from universality and the game's boundary conditions

nodes.statement: In about fifty years, it will be possible to program computers to play the imitation game so well that an average interrogator will have no more than a 70 percent chance of making the right identification.
nodes.span: I believe that in about fifty years' time it will be possible, to programme computers
nodes.status_reason: Turing's personal conjecture about the future

nodes.statement: The theological objection implies a serious restriction on God's omnipotence, as God should have the freedom to confer a soul on a machine.
nodes.span: It appears to me that the argument quoted above implies a serious restriction of the omnipotence of the Almighty.
nodes.status_reason: follows from basic logic regarding omnipotence

nodes.statement: The 'heads in the sand' objection is based on a desire for human superiority and is not substantial enough to require refutation.
nodes.span: I do not think that this argument is sufficiently substantial to require refutation.
nodes.status_reason: follows from basic logic that fear of a consequence does not make a claim false

nodes.statement: Mathematical logic shows there are limitations to any particular discrete-state machine, meaning there are questions it will answer wrongly or not at all.
nodes.span: It states that there are certain things that such a machine cannot do.
nodes.status_reason: reader does not hold Gödel's incompleteness theorems or Turing's halting problem

nodes.statement: The mathematical objection fails because there is no proof that the human intellect is not subject to similar limitations, and triumphing over one machine does not mean triumphing over all.
nodes.span: it has only been stated, without any sort of proof, that no such limitations apply to the human intellect.
nodes.status_reason: follows from basic logic that human infallibility is unproven

nodes.statement: The argument from consciousness logically leads to an extreme solipsist position where one can only know if they themselves think.
nodes.span: the only way by which one could be sure that machine thinks is to be the machine
nodes.status_reason: follows from basic logic applied to knowing others' minds

nodes.statement: If proponents of the consciousness argument abandon solipsism, they will likely accept the imitation game as a valid viva voce test.
nodes.span: most of those who support the argument from consciousness could be persuaded to abandon it rather than be forced into the solipsist position.
nodes.status_reason: follows from rejecting solipsism

nodes.statement: Arguments that machines cannot do specific things are largely based on flawed scientific induction from observing limited, low-capacity machines.
nodes.span: I believe they are mostly founded on the principle of scientific induction.
nodes.status_reason: follows from reader's knowledge of informal probability and induction

nodes.statement: The claim that machines cannot make mistakes confuses mechanical errors of functioning with errors of conclusion, the latter of which machines can certainly make.
nodes.span: It seems to me that this criticism depends on a confusion between two kinds of mistake
nodes.status_reason: follows from basic logic distinguishing mechanical faults from false outputs

nodes.statement: A machine can be the subject of its own thought by observing its behavior and modifying its own programs to achieve a purpose.
nodes.span: By observing the results of its own behaviour it can modify its own programmes so as to achieve some purpose more effectively.
nodes.status_reason: reader holds that programs can process data, including their own instructions

nodes.statement: Lady Lovelace's objection that computers cannot originate anything only reflects that the evidence available to her did not encourage belief in this property.
nodes.span: the evidence available to Lady Lovelace did not encourage her to believe that they had it.
nodes.status_reason: follows from basic logic regarding absence of evidence

nodes.statement: The variant objection that machines cannot take us by surprise is false, as machines frequently surprise their creators.
nodes.span: Machines take me by surprise with great frequency.
nodes.status_reason: Turing's personal testimony of being surprised

nodes.statement: Although the nervous system is continuous, a digital computer can mimic continuous systems well enough that the interrogator cannot take advantage of the difference.
nodes.span: if we adhere to the conditions of the imitation game, the interrogator will not be able to take any advantage of this difference.
nodes.status_reason: reader holds informal probability and understands mimicking

nodes.statement: The argument that humans are not machines because they lack complete rules of conduct confuses conscious precepts with natural laws of behavior.
nodes.span: There may however be a certain confusion between "rules of conduct" and "laws of behaviour" to cloud the issue.
nodes.status_reason: follows from basic logic distinguishing conscious rules from natural laws

nodes.statement: We cannot prove the absence of complete laws of behavior for humans, just as we cannot easily predict the behavior of a complex discrete-state machine from observation.
nodes.span: given a discrete-state machine it should certainly be possible to discover by observation sufficient about it to predict its future behaviour
nodes.status_reason: follows from basic logic that exhaustive search of laws is impossible

nodes.statement: If extrasensory perception is admitted, the imitation game must be tightened by placing competitors in a telepathy-proof room.
nodes.span: If telepathy is admitted it will be necessary to tighten our test up.
nodes.status_reason: follows from basic logic of experimental controls

nodes.statement: Instead of trying to program an adult mind directly, it is more promising to program a child machine and subject it to an education process.
nodes.span: Instead of trying to produce a programme to simulate the adult mind, why not rather try to produce one which simulates the child's?
nodes.status_reason: proposed method for programming

nodes.statement: The process of teaching a child machine is analogous to evolution, mapping structure to hereditary material, changes to mutations, and judgment to natural selection.
nodes.span: There is an obvious connection between this process and evolution
nodes.status_reason: follows from basic logic mapping machine components to biology

nodes.statement: Artificial evolution will be faster than biological evolution because the experimenter can use intelligence to guide mutations.
nodes.span: One may hope, however, that this process will be more expeditious than evolution.
nodes.status_reason: follows from basic logic that guided search is faster than random

nodes.statement: Teaching a machine requires unemotional channels of communication, like a symbolic language, in addition to punishments and rewards.
nodes.span: It is necessary therefore to have some other "unemotional" channels of communication.
nodes.status_reason: follows from basic logic regarding information bandwidth

nodes.statement: The rules of a learning machine can change without violating the definition of a machine because the changing rules have only ephemeral validity.
nodes.span: The explanation of the paradox is that the rules which get changed in the learning process are of a rather less pretentious kind
nodes.status_reason: follows from reader's knowledge of rules and basic logic

nodes.statement: Intelligent behavior consists in a slight departure from completely disciplined computation, allowing flexibility without becoming completely random.
nodes.span: Intelligent behaviour presumably consists in a departure from the completely disciplined behaviour involved in computation
nodes.status_reason: follows from basic logic regarding strict rules vs flexibility

nodes.statement: Including a random element in a learning machine is useful for searching for solutions.
nodes.span: It is probably wise to include a random element in a learning machine.
nodes.status_reason: reader holds informal probability
